title: Agentic AI is a loop, not a menu
dek: Five layers, built one exhibit at a time, in the order you should actually reach for them.
audience: Someone about to choose between RAG, an agent, and a protocol

beats.title: These are layers, not rivals — and they arrive in one order
paragraphs: RAG, agents, MCP, and A2A are not competing products. They are layers, and each one exists because the layer below it cannot reach something.
Understand, find, act, orchestrate. That is the order they arrive in, and the order you should buy them in.
beats.exhibit: The five layers of the agentic stack
beats.takeaway: Buy the layer your problem needs, not the layer the pitch deck sells.
beats.annotation: Understand → find → act → orchestrate is also the buying order.
notes: Open on the model alone. Nothing else on the exhibit yet.
The promise of the next four minutes: by the end you can name the thinnest layer that solves your problem.
Warn them now that most teams need fewer layers than the pitch deck suggests.

beats.title: A model is language, and nothing else
paragraphs: Prompted chat turns your words into more words. It has no library and no hands, so anything it does not already contain, it fills in.
Every layer after this one is added because language alone cannot reach something outside itself.
beats.exhibit: Layer 1 — a prompted model: words in, words out
beats.takeaway: If prompted chat already answers the question, that is the whole system.
beats.annotation: No library and no hands: anything outside the prompt gets filled in.
notes: Point at the prompt going in and the answer coming out. That is the entire layer.
Memory check line one: LLM equals language.
Nobody is wrong to stop here. Plenty of useful work is prompted chat.

beats.title: Give it a library before you give it hands
paragraphs: Answers that ignore your documents, go stale, or invent policy are a knowledge problem. The fix is retrieval: find the passage, answer from it, cite it.
An internal policy bot quoting the current refund SOP needs a library, not autonomy.
beats.exhibit: Layer 2 — retrieval grounds the answer in your own documents
beats.takeaway: Most things pitched as an agent are a retrieval problem.
beats.annotation: Ask how entities link rather than what a passage says, and you want GraphRAG.
notes: Documents are placed in reading order, then the retrieve-and-cite path is drawn back up into the answer.
Memory check line two: RAG equals library.
First anti-pattern: reaching for an agent to do pure question and answer.
If the question is about how entities link rather than what a passage says, that is where GraphRAG comes in.

beats.title: The loop is what makes it an agent
paragraphs: Plan, act, observe, stop. A model sitting in a fixed pipeline is a workflow no matter how many prompts it has; it becomes an agent when it chooses the next step and decides when to quit.
Earn this layer with work that branches and retries — a month-end expense pack, not a question.
beats.exhibit: Layer 3 — the control loop: plan, act, observe, stop
beats.takeaway: If the path is fixed, you have a workflow, and a workflow is cheaper.
beats.annotation: Code owns the order in a workflow; the model owns the order in an agent.
notes: Trace the cycle once with a finger while the token runs it.
The distinction to leave them with: code owns the order in a workflow, the model owns the order in an agent.
Calling a fixed pipeline an agent is on the anti-pattern list.

beats.title: If you can’t stop it, you don’t ship it
paragraphs: A loop that spends money or writes to production runs behind caps: max steps, max euros and tokens, and a tool allowlist.
Where the write is irreversible, the loop pauses and waits for a human.
beats.exhibit: Always on — the human gate and the caps around the loop
beats.takeaway: Caps and a human Approve are the price of letting a loop touch money.
beats.annotation: A refund over €50 pauses here, and step caps stop a runaway.
notes: The token reaches the bar and waits. Let the pause sit for a second; the pause is the point.
Caps first, Approve second. The caps are what stop a runaway; Approve is what keeps you accountable.
This beat is the one delivery people remember. Do not rush it.

beats.title: Tools are reach, not knowledge
paragraphs: A retrieval index cannot tell you today’s stock level. Live reads and writes are a tools problem: the loop calls the system and gets the current answer.
The protocol earns its place when the same tools must serve several apps.
beats.exhibit: Layer 4 — one tool contract, four live systems
beats.takeaway: RAG and MCP are not alternatives: one is the library, the other the hands.
beats.annotation: One service calling two APIs is a function call, not a protocol.
notes: The trunk leaves the cycle, the bus fans out, and answers come back up the drops. Reach, not memory.
Memory check line three: MCP equals hands.
Kill the either-or question early — RAG and MCP are not alternatives.

beats.title: Peers only when the boundary is real
paragraphs: Two agents owned by different teams or vendors, each keeping its own tools, need a way to hand work across. That is what A2A is for.
Inside one codebase it is a function call with ceremony. Premature swarms are on the anti-pattern list.
beats.exhibit: Layer 5 — a handoff across an ownership boundary
beats.takeaway: A2A is for agents that different teams or vendors own; anything less is premature.
beats.annotation: Support hands a refund packet to finance-ops; each side keeps its own tools.
notes: The dashed rule is an ownership boundary, not a network hop.
Support hands a refund packet to finance-ops across two tenants. Each side keeps its own MCP tools.
If the two agents have one owner, you do not have a boundary.

beats.title: Climb it in order, and stop early
paragraphs: Six rungs, and the card publishes them in order. Each one is added only when the rung below it cannot reach the job.
The exhibit beside this list is every layer at once — which is what the top rung costs, and why the card says to earn it.
beats.exhibit: The assembled stack, all five layers at once
beats.takeaway: The top rung says “earn this”, and most teams never need to.
beats.annotation: Default order: chat, retrieval, one agent with tools, a gate, many, then A2A.
notes: Six rungs. Read them out; the order is the argument.
The exhibit has no highlight now on purpose — this is the whole stack, and the whole stack is the expensive answer.
Ask the room which rung they are on, and which rung they were sold.

beats.title: Start at the thinnest layer that solves the job
paragraphs: Find the row that matches the real problem and take the layer it names — nothing above it. The card below has eleven of those rows.
Behaviour sits across all of it: rules are standing orders, skills are runbooks. LLM is language, RAG is the library, MCP is the hands.
beats.exhibit: What most teams actually need, with the rest faded back
beats.takeaway: Name the thinnest layer that solves your job, and buy nothing above it.
beats.annotation: Rules are standing orders; skills are runbooks. Both sit across every layer.
notes: The peer row fades back. What is left is the honest architecture for most teams.
Hand them the card as the reference and keep this deck as the briefing.
Last line: a rule that belongs in a skill is still a mistake, even when the stack is right.

closing.title: The deck briefs; the card decides
paragraphs: This is the same material as the published field card, paced for a first meeting with it. Nothing here is asserted that the card does not already say — each section names the rows it teaches, and the build fails if one of those rows disappears.
The card stays the thing you keep open during a design review. It is reprinted below, from the same frozen source this deck reads.
